concrete_recipe:
GOAL: a small fine-tuned "pointer" VLM that answers CubiCasa raster count questions (53% of all preview questions) with one numbered point per object. Claude stays the router, the text-answer model and the fallback. IFC, DXF and Swiss questions stay on the native $0 tools.

HARDWARE: 1x A100 80GB ($2.37/h) for everything. Optionally a second A100 for parallel baselines. Do not use V100s: no bf16, and current vLLM likely needs compute capability >= 7.5. The chili RTX 5090 (free) can serve the final 4B model.

H0-3 (CPU, local) - data builder.
1. Download CubiCasa5K (5.5 GB, Zenodo 2613548). Parse model.svg with the logic in CubiCasa's house.py.
   - Door and window midpoints come from id='Door' / id='Window' polygons.
   - Icon centroids come from 'FixedFurniture X' (Toilet, Sink*, Bathtub*, Shower*, SaunaBench*/SaunaStove).
   - Room label points come from 'Space X' polygons (Bedroom, Bath, Sauna, Kitchen, and so on).
   - Check how storeys/floors are encoded in the SVG.
2. Map every preview question template (EN + Finnish) to one SVG query. Generate targets in Molmo style: points sorted top-down, left-to-right, then the count. Coordinates are 0-1000 relative (Qwen3.x convention), with no reasoning text (Perception-R1: thinking hurts counting).
3. CALIBRATE: match the preview cubicasa drawings to CubiCasa5K IDs. Compare the SVG-derived counts with Stoa's answers for each type. Fix definitions until agreement is at least 95% (for example "door with leaf", "showers+bathtubs", which room codes count as KH/PH/PESUH/SH).
4. HOLD OUT every drawing that appears in questions.jsonl (preview, and full set when available) plus the CubiCasa test split. Train only on the rest: about 4k images x about 8 questions = about 30k samples. Add about 10% negative questions where the answer is 0 and there are no points.

H2-5 (A100, in parallel with step 3) - zero-shot baselines on 500 held-out preview count questions with vLLM.
- Models: Molmo2-4B and Molmo2-8B (native counting-by-pointing; PixMo-Count 88.1/88.5), and Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B with a "point to each X, return JSON point_2d" prompt.
- Compare with the current Claude point-placement pipeline: exact-match rate and $/question.
- This gives the first real accuracy number and selects the base model.

H5-11 - SFT.
- Base: Qwen3.5-4B (Apache-2.0). Fallback: Qwen3-VL-4B, or Qwen2.5-VL-3B (best tested in TRL, VLM-R1 and PR1).
- Tool: Unsloth FastVisionModel, or LLaMA-Factory with template qwen3_5.
- Settings: LoRA r=32, alpha=64, on language plus vision layers (grounding benefits from an unfrozen vision tower). lr 1e-4 to 2e-4, 1 epoch, bf16. Image max about 1.6 MP (about 1.5k visual tokens). Very large plans are tiled into 2x2 overlapping crops with points merged by radius.
- Expected VRAM is about 10-30 GB. Time is ESTIMATED at 3-5 h for 20-30k samples (not measured; cut to 15k samples if throughput is low).
- Merge the LoRA into the base weights. vLLM cannot apply LoRA to vision layers.

H11-13 - evaluation on the held-out set.
- Exact match per question type, point precision/recall (Hungarian matching, radius = 1.5% of the image diagonal), and failure gallery images for the UI.

H13-21 (optional, only if doors and windows still lag) - GRPO/GSPO.
- Tool: TRL GRPOTrainer or Unsloth (vision layers frozen when vLLM generates).
- Reward = 1.0 x exact count + 0.5 x point F1 (Hungarian) + 0.2 x format - duplicate penalty. These are the PointRL and Perception-R1 terms.
- Run on about 2k hard prompts where the SFT model was wrong. 8 generations, lr 1e-6 to 5e-6, KL 0-0.04, about 300 steps.
- ESTIMATED 4-6 h on 1-2 A100s. Stop early if held-out accuracy does not rise within 100 steps.

H21-28 - serving.
- Run vLLM (A100 or chili 5090) behind a Drawing Desk tool point_count(image, class) -> numbered points.
- Use the vLLM prefix cache, so all questions on one drawing share the image prefill.
- Confidence check: two samples (or full image vs tiles), plus a Florence-2-large detector count if time allows. If the counts disagree, escalate to Claude Opus with the candidate points drawn on the image.
- The UI shows numbered dots and lets the user add or remove a point to recount. This gives judges the verifiable-reasoning view.

H28-34 - pitch numbers.
- Report accuracy (held-out) and $/question for each route. Publish the weights on HF as a non-commercial derivative and name the Verda training run.

EXPECTED ACCURACY: no published number exists for this task. The references:
- Frontier models score 0.40-0.55 on door/window counting (AECV-Bench).
- Molmo2-4B reaches 88% on natural-image PixMo-Count.
- In-domain RL took a 2B model from 50.5% to 75.6% on PixMo-Count.
- Hypothesis to verify at H11: at least 90% exact on low-count icon classes (WC, sink, sauna, kitchen) and 70-85% on doors and windows, about 85% over all CubiCasa counts.

COST (ESTIMATES):
- Training total about $20-40: SFT about $10, GRPO about $12, baselines and eval about $10.
- Self-hosted 4B on A100: at a conservative 3-10 questions/s with about 1.5k image tokens and 100-300 output tokens, $2.37/3600/(3-10) = about $0.00007-0.0002 per question. This holds only while the GPU is busy. An idle A100 costs $57/day, which is why the chili box matters.
- Claude Opus 5.5 ($4/$20 per MTok): a single call with about 3.5k input and about 1.5k output (points plus thinking) costs about $0.045. A 3-5 turn tool loop costs about $0.1-0.3.
- Claude Haiku 5.5 ($0.10/$0.50): about $0.001.
- So the fine-tuned pointer is about 200-1000x cheaper than Opus and about 5-15x cheaper than Haiku 5.5, and it is more accurate only if the H11 eval shows it.
risks: Train/test leakage and integrity: the cubicasa5k drawings in the Stoa set very likely ARE CubiCasa5K images, and the answers were likely derived from the same SVGs. Training on their annotations inflates scores, and judges may treat it as cheating. Exclude every drawing that appears in questions.jsonl from training. Report only held-out accuracy, and state this in the pitch.

Licence: CubiCasa5K is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so the fine-tuned weights are effectively non-commercial and share-alike. Molmo2 training data also contains non-commercial sources, and Visual-RFT data is CC BY-NC. This is acceptable for a hackathon demo, but must be disclosed to Stoa (work-trial context).

Label-definition mismatch between the SVG classes and Stoa's templates (doors with leaf, showers+bathtubs grouping, KH/PH/PESUH/SH room codes, storeys, windows drawn as one or several segments). Without calibration against the 4,270 preview pairs, the model learns the wrong definition and exact-match accuracy collapses.

Tooling newness: Qwen3.5 is a Gated DeltaNet hybrid. TRL's tested VLM list does not include Qwen3-VL or Qwen3.5, and Unsloth's vision-RL page does not name Qwen3.5. Budget 1 h to smoke-test SFT and GRPO, then fall back to Qwen3-VL-4B or Qwen2.5-VL-3B.

vLLM cannot apply LoRA to vision layers, so merge before serving. During vLLM-backed GRPO the vision tower must stay frozen. Molmo2 repo fine-tuning is full-parameter only (no LoRA mentioned) and uses 8-GPU examples.
V100 is a trap: no bf16, no FlashAttention 2, and current vLLM reportedly needs compute capability >= 7.5. Use A100 or the RTX 5090.

Small symbols on large plans: downscaling to about 1.5 MP can erase door swings and WC symbols. Tiling fixes recall but creates duplicate points at tile seams, which need radius-based merging. Coordinate bugs are common (Qwen2.5-VL absolute pixels vs Qwen3.x relative 0-1000; Qwen3-VL users report values above 1000).

Over-promising: Perception-R1's generic SFT gave no counting gain, and Blueprint2CAD found LoRA adds only a few points on hard drawing tasks. In-domain SFT on dense point labels should do better, but nothing is measured until H11. Keep the Claude point-placement pipeline as the fallback.
Time: GRPO can consume 8+ hours for little gain. Gate it on the H11 eval and stop if held-out accuracy is flat after 100 steps.

Cost narrative: the advantage over Claude Haiku 5.5 is only about 5-15x, and per-question GPU cost assumes a saturated GPU. An idle A100 at $57/day loses to API calls at low volume. Present both numbers, and serve from the free chili box.

Coverage gaps: historic scans (habs, finna, europeana, wikimedia) and US vector drawing sets are out of distribution for a CubiCasa-trained pointer. Route them to Claude and the native tools, not the fine-tune.
Some sources (MolmoPoint weights, AECV-Bench per-model numbers, FloorplanVLM base model) could not be confirmed from the pages fetched. Treat those details as unverified.

track: Research landscape: question answering over AEC drawings and BIM (2024-2026). Covers benchmarks, frontier VLM scores, failure modes, hybrid methods that win, and IFC-Bench v2 grading.

key_findings.title: AECV-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Models on Architectural and Engineering Drawings Understanding (Kondratenko, Birhane, Hsain, Maciocci)
key_findings.year: 2026 (arXiv v1 8 Jan 2026; repo results updated through current models)
key_findings.what: There are two tasks. (1) Counting doors, windows, spaces, bedrooms and toilets on 120 floor plans, scored by per-field exact match and MAPE. (2) 192 drawing-grounded QA pairs in four groups: OCR, instance counting, spatial and comparative. An LLM judge (GPT-4o) grades them, and humans settle edge cases. The abstract says OCR/text QA reaches up to 0.95 accuracy, while door and window counting 'remains unsolved (often 0.40-0.55)'. We recomputed exact-match accuracy from the repo CSVs, which show per-field results for current models. Door/Window/Bedroom/Toilet: Gemini 3.5 Flash 0.43/0.39/0.93/0.82 (MAPE door 12%, window 17%). Gemini 3 Pro 0.40/0.34/0.89/0.83. Claude Fable 5 0.36/0.29/0.93/0.82. GPT-5.5 0.30/0.28/0.93/0.77. Claude Opus 4.8 0.15/0.15/0.88/0.77. Claude Opus 4.5 0.16/0.16/0.91/0.76. Qwen3-VL-8B 0.09/0.10/0.76/0.81. 'Space' (room count) is 0.13-0.27 for every model. Cost per run of 120 plans: Fable 5 $9.22 ($0.077/plan, 29 s mean latency), GPT-5.5 $26.88 ($0.22/plan, 182 s), Gemini 3.5 Flash $3.77 ($0.031/plan).
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This is the closest public match to the 76% raster-count slice. It shows that the strongest frontier VLMs get door/window counts exactly right on only about 30-43% of plans. Bedroom and toilet counts reach about 80-93%, because they come from labels and few, large symbols. So 'Claude places points' is a weak baseline for doors, windows and rooms, and a trained detector is where the accuracy is. The per-plan cost numbers also give a direct cost comparison for the low-inference-cost criterion.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: The code, the 120 images, the ground truth and every model's raw outputs are public on GitHub. The repo has no LICENSE file, so reuse rights are unclear.

key_findings.title: BIM Information Extraction Through LLM-based Adaptive Exploration (Hellin, Jang, Fuchs, Nousias, Borrmann, TU Munich) - introduces ifc-bench v2
key_findings.what: ifc-bench v2 has 1,027 QA tasks over 37 IFC models from 21 projects (Revit/ArchiCAD; IFC2X3, IFC4, IFC4X3). There are four categories: C1 direct retrieval, C2 aggregation/counting, C3 geometric/spatial, C4 incomplete information. The test split is a fixed 514 questions. The method is a CodeAct agent that writes IfcOpenShell Python in a sandbox, iterates, and abstains when it hits the iteration cap. GLM-4.7 (355B total, 32B active) scores 56.0% with no augmentation, against 19.1% for a static one-shot query (+37 pp, p<0.001). GLM-4.5-Air (106B/12B active) scores 25.7%. Doc retrieval, hand-written tools and auto-generated tools change the strong model by at most 0.6 pp, which is not significant. Per category for GLM-4.7: C1 55.6%, C2 53.4%, C3 66.7%, C4 57.8%. Materials questions reach only 42%. Per-project accuracy ranges from 25% to 90%.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Stoa's ifc_bench slice (249 free-text questions on 5 models) comes from this benchmark. Frontier agents score only about 55-60% on it, so an IfcOpenShell agent that explores step by step clearly beats one-shot query generation. Hand-written tools did not help a strong model. The paper's judge rubric is the de facto grading method for these free-text answers.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code: https://github.com/sylvainHellin/cobbie (CC BY 4.0). Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/sylvainHellin/ifc-bench (QA CC BY 4.0; each IFC keeps its own licence, and four models are GPLv3). Agents run through API models, so there are no weights.

key_findings.title: How IFC-Bench v2 free-text answers are graded (cobbie answer_verifier.baml)
key_findings.what: The grader is an LLM judge that sees the question, category, ground truth, system answer and execution trace. It first decides whether the system abstained. If not, it judges four binary criteria: faithfulness, completeness, transparency and relevance. Faithfulness rules for C1/C2: continuous values (length, area, volume) must be within 2% of the reference, and counts must match exactly. For C3, methodology must be disclosed and values must be plausible. For C4, assumptions must be stated. Transparency means every claim cites a specific property, method or assumption, for example '24 windows counted IfcWindow elements'. An answer is correct only if criteria 1-4 pass. In the repo, the default judge client in answer_verifier.baml is GLM_4_7. scripts/run_second_llm_judge.py adds a judge from a second family. The paper reports judge agreement of Krippendorff alpha 0.70-1.00, against 0.32-0.57 between human experts. The ONESTRUCTION Construction AI Leaderboard (7 Nov 2026) notes that the public code lets the model grade itself by default, so it fixed the judge to DeepSeek-V3.2. Its runs allow 15 code runs per question on the 514 test questions.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: The Stoa scoring rules (counts exact, area/length/volume within 2%) match the ifc-bench rubric exactly, so Stoa probably follows it. To grade the 'text' type, we can copy this rubric with Haiku as judge. Our answers should also be written to pass 'transparency': name the IFC class and property, or the quantity set, behind each number. Drawing Desk citations already work this way.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Judge prompt and scripts are public under CC BY 4.0.

key_findings.title: Construction AI Leaderboard (ONESTRUCTION, Hugging Face blog)
key_findings.what: It covers five axes: AEC-Bench (drawings), BIM-Edit, IFC-Bench-V2, CEQuest and Ishigaki-IDS-Bench. Overall scores: Claude Opus 5.5 73.7, Gemini 4 Argon 73.6, Claude Opus 5 72.7, GPT-6.1 Sol 70.2, Sonnet 5.5 66.9. On AEC-Bench drawings, Opus 5.5 scores 70.2 at $0.33 and 1.7 min per task, and Sonnet 5.5 scores 58.6 at $0.14. Claude Opus 5 ranks first on IFC-Bench-V2, but the blog text gives no number for it.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: These are current-generation results for the exact models we have. Opus 5.5 is the strongest drawing/document agent, and its per-task cost is useful for a cost comparison with our router.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Not applicable (a leaderboard).

key_findings.title: AEC-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Agentic Systems in AEC (Galanos/Aurecon, Mulyar/Nomic AI)
key_findings.what: 196 tasks in 9 families over real public drawing sets, specs and submittals: intra-sheet, intra-drawing and intra-project. Each is scored by an automated verifier with partial credit. Agents tested: Claude Code (Opus/Sonnet 4.6) and Codex (GPT-5.4/5.2), with and without Nomic parse/embedding tools. Note-callout defects that text can catch score 100%, but defects that need visual inspection score about 5%, and rendering images did not help. The best submittal-review score is 23.1. 77% of trajectories used pdftotext, which loses layout.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This confirms that agents fail on visual-spatial grounding, such as leader lines and matching text to geometry. It supports our approach of keeping text spans with bounding boxes from the vector PDF, not plain pdftotext.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Dataset, harness and evaluation are public under Apache-2.0.

key_findings.title: DrawingVQA: real-world benchmark on construction drawings (Jung, Fu, Golparvar-Fard)
key_findings.what: 92 expert-written QA pairs (mostly multiple choice) on 33 issued-for-construction structural drawings. Overall: Gemini-3-pro 77.2%, Gemini-2.5-pro 71.7%, o3 58.7%, Claude-4.5-Sonnet 57.6%, Qwen3-VL-8B 53.3%, GPT-4o 48.9%. Professionals score 94.9%. Quantity takeoff (counting) is the weakest dimension for every model, at 0-58% on a small subset. Without the image, o3 drops to 29.5% and Gemini-2.5-flash to 9.8%. Failure modes: losing its place while tracing grid lines during counting, taking a callout from the neighbouring symbol, and stopping cross-referencing at the first plausible link.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This is more independent evidence that counting and quantity takeoff is where frontier VLMs break. It also shows that visible grounding (which symbol was counted) is what lets a human catch the error.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/S2-MIND/DrawingVQA (CC BY-NC-SA family licence). The paper names no code repo.

key_findings.title: Getting to the Point: Pointing Improves LVLMs at Counting (Alghisi et al.)
key_findings.what: Point-then-Count (PtC): the model outputs coordinates first, then the count. After LoRA fine-tuning (rank 32, single A100 80GB, at most 2 days per experiment), PtC reaches about 99.9-100% in-distribution on synthetic data. On real OCID data PtC scores 76-82%, against 69-75% for direct counting. Out of distribution, counting the predicted points is much better than the model's stated final count. On synthetic OOD data, InternVL3.5-8B scores 97.9% when you count its points, against 45.5% for direct counting. Zero-shot, Molmo-7B-O gets 99.95% with PtC against 53% with direct counting.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This validates Drawing Desk's rule that count = len(points). It also shows that a small VLM fine-tuned to point at symbols is a viable trained component. Always count the emitted points, never the model's stated number.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: https://github.com/sislab-unitn/Getting-to-the-Point (CC BY 4.0).

key_findings.title: SAM 3: Segment Anything with Concepts (Meta)
key_findings.what: An open-vocabulary concept segmenter. The table as reported by a third-party site gives CountBench 93.8% accuracy (MAE 0.12) against Gemini 2.5 Pro 92.4%, and PixMo-Count 86.2% against Molmo-72B 88.8%. Ultralytics docs give 95.6% and 87.3%. Only the 2-10 object range is tested.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: It is a zero-training fallback detector for 'count all X'. Prompt it with 'toilet' or 'door', or with an exemplar crop, and it returns masks we can draw as evidence. It is untested on line-art floor plans, so measure it on CubiCasa before relying on it.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Weights released by Meta under the SAM licence. Also packaged in Ultralytics.

key_findings.title: Automated Facility Enumeration using Door Detection and LLMs (Zhang, Le, Akhtar, Ngo, U. Melbourne)
key_findings.what: A Co-DETR detector feeds an LLM to count facilities across 8 floor-plan datasets. On CubiCasa5K toilet counting: 87.63% against GPT-5 at 85.57%. On kitchen: 98.97% against 96.91%. The gains are largest on unusual drawing styles, for example CVC-FP 86.7% against 40.0% and SESYD 95.8% against 68.8%.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This is a published detector-plus-LLM hybrid on the same CubiCasa source that beats a frontier VLM on counting. The largest gains come on plan styles outside the training data, which matters for 14,000 drawings from mixed sources.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: No code. The authors say the labels will be released later.

key_findings.title: CubiCasa5K dataset (Kalervo et al.) and derived detection sets
key_findings.what: 5,000 Finnish floor plans with dense SVG polygon annotations in more than 80 categories: rooms with type labels, doors, windows and icons such as toilet, sink, shower, bathtub and sauna bench. The split is about 4,200/400/400. The Zenodo zip is 5.47 GB, licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The original repo has a pretrained multi-task CNN with weights on Google Drive. Derivatives: HF v1nz/cubicasa5k-yolo (wall/door/window YOLO polygons, 1.76 GB, CC BY-NC 4.0, no icons). Roboflow cubicasa5k-2 has an RF-DETR-Base door/window/wall model at mAP50 74.6% (May 2025). TextCAD (arXiv 2607.12678) maps CubiCasa to 10 countable thing classes plus wall and railing.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Stoa's cubicasa5k slice is these plans, with question types that match the CubiCasa labels: WC seats, sinks, showers/bathtubs, saunas, doors, windows, room types. Training a detector and segmenter on the SVG ground truth is the most direct fix for the biggest accuracy gap. Some Stoa drawings may also be in CubiCasa train/val/test. Check by hash and hold those out, so accuracy measurements stay honest.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Data: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial). Original model weights on Google Drive. The GitHub repo licence is listed as 'Other'.

key_findings.title: Grounded and Faithful P&ID Reasoning: Constraining VLMs with Recovered Evidence Graphs (Gadekar, Sakhinana, Runkana)
key_findings.what: Pipeline: tiled symbol detection, then U-Net line masks, skeleton vectorization, YOLO text detection with fine-tuned TrOCR, and a connection graph. The VLM may only answer through 7 read-only graph operators and must cite their results. On TopoPID-VQA (3,000 topology questions), exact match rises from 36.7-41.3% with images only to 74.3-76.0%, using Qwen3-VL-4B/8B and Gemma-4-E4B. The remaining errors come from mistakes in the recovered graph.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This is the clearest 2026 evidence for Stoa's thesis. CV extracts a structured evidence graph, a small model queries it, and the cited query results are the visual proof. It is the same pattern as our IFC/DXF tools, extended to rasters.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: No code link. The paper is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

key_findings.title: FloorplanQA: spatial reasoning in LLMs using structured representations (Rodionov et al.)
key_findings.what: 2,000 symbolic layouts (JSON/XML) and 16,000 QA pairs in 8 task types: distance, visibility, path finding, free space, placement and others. Ground truth is computed with shapely and A*. 15 LLMs are tested. The hardest tasks are free space, maximal rectangle and shortest path. Models fail at centroids of complex polygons. Giving the model a Python tool fixes the arithmetic errors.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Once a drawing is vectorized into polygons, do area and geometry in code (shapely), not in the LLM. This supports deterministic area tools for swiss_dwellings and ifc_models.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code public on GitHub. Licence not checked.

key_findings.title: AECBench (ECADI + Tongji)
key_findings.what: A Chinese text-only benchmark on AEC knowledge at 5 cognitive levels: memorization, understanding, reasoning, calculation, application. Across 9 LLMs, scores fall at each higher level. Models do worst on tables in building codes, calculations and document generation.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: It is only indirectly relevant, because it has no drawings. It shows that calculation and table lookup are weak points, which supports doing arithmetic in tools.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/jackluoluo/AECBench (CC BY-NC 4.0).

key_findings.title: ArchCAD-400K and DPSS symbol spotter (Luo et al., Tongji); SymPointV2
key_findings.what: 413,062 chunks from 5,538 vector CAD drawings, 27 categories, line-level labels created by an automatic engine. The Dual-Pathway Symbol Spotter reaches 40.7% instance-spotting mAP, against SymPointV2 39.7% and SymPoint 30.8%. SymPointV2 works on SVG primitives and has weights on Google Drive.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: These are the reference methods for counting symbols directly from vector primitives: DXF, and vector PDF from opening_design. The mAP is only about 40%, so on vector files, block names and layers (our DXF tools) are more reliable than learned spotting.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: ArchCAD data: CC BY-NC 4.0 on HF (jackluoluo/ArchCAD, 2.63 GB). DPSS code on GitHub. SymPointV2 has weights but no licence file.

key_findings.title: Fine-Tuning VLM for Engineering Drawing Information Extraction (Khan et al.)
key_findings.what: Florence-2 (0.23B parameters), fully fine-tuned on 400 GD&T-annotated mechanical drawings. Against the better of GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet zero-shot: F1 +52.4%, precision +29.95%, recall +37.75%, hallucination rate -43.15%. Training compute is not reported.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: A small fine-tuned VLM beats frontier models on a narrow drawing extraction task with only 400 examples. This supports 'small fine-tuned model + frontier orchestrator', and Florence-2 is cheap to train on a V100.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: No code or weights linked. The paper is CC BY 4.0.

key_findings.title: Natural Language Information Retrieval from BIM Models (Hellin, Nousias, Borrmann, EC3 2025) - IFC-Bench v1
key_findings.what: A ReAct agent with 29 hand-coded IfcOpenShell tools, working directly on IFC files: 80% on 99 queries, and 95% when the information exists directly in the model. Related systems: BIM-GPT (arXiv 2304.09333, prompt-based retrieval), Text2BIM (arXiv 2408.08054, multi-agent model generation, not QA), and BIMCoder (reported 87.16% match / 88.75% execution accuracy).
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Accuracy collapses when questions move from direct lookups (about 95%) to computation and incomplete information (v2: about 55%). Our deterministic Qto/storey/space selectors cover the easy part at $0. An agent fallback with tool loops is needed for the long tail.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: IFC-Bench v1 is in the same HF dataset (CC BY 4.0). The v1 GitHub repo is archived at https://github.com/sylvainHellin/ifc-bench.

key_findings.title: MSD / Swiss Dwellings (van Engelenburg et al., ECCV 2024)
key_findings.what: Swiss Dwellings v3.0.0 (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.7788422): a dataframe of WKT polygons in metres for every room, wall, opening and balcony, with site/building/plan/floor/apartment/unit IDs and room types. MSD has 5,372 floor plans with a building-level train/test split. Both are CC BY 4.0.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: The swiss_dwellings slice is rendered from this geometry. Room areas and counts can be computed exactly from the DXF/PDF vectors with shapely. The public dataframe lets us check our area extractor against the true polygons and the 2% tolerance.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Data CC BY 4.0. Tooling AGPL.

key_findings.title: Other 2026 drawing benchmarks found (context)
key_findings.what: MechVQA (ICML 2026, arXiv 2605.30794): 3.3K mechanical drawings and 21K QA. Its fine-tuned MechVL beats the best closed model by 7.57 pp. Base model and compute are not given on the abstract page. MMArch (arXiv 2608.09281): 1,212 items. Best proprietary MLLM 52%, best open model about 30%, experts 95%. IFCMemoryBench (arXiv 2607.26072), BIM-Edit (arXiv 2606.20146) and BIBIMBAP (arXiv 2611.09933) are BIM agent benchmarks. We found no papers named 'BlueprintQA', 'CAD-VQA', 'ArchiText' or 'DrawingQA'. The closest real ones are AECV-Bench, DrawingVQA and FloorplanQA.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: The pattern is the same in every domain: fine-tuned small models or tool-grounded pipelines beat zero-shot frontier models on symbol-dense drawings, and the gap to human experts stays large.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: MechVQA code link was promised in v2 but not found. MMArch project page: https://dcx-swjtu.github.io/MMArch/

concrete_recipe:
Goal: put a trained CV layer under the 76% raster-count slice, and keep the frontier model for routing, edge cases and explanation. The thesis comes from the literature (P&ID evidence graph +35 pp, adaptive IFC agent +37 pp, detector+LLM beats GPT-5 on CubiCasa): CV/geometry builds structured, citable evidence, and a model only queries it.

STEP 0 (hours 0-2, laptop). Build a harness on the preview set (7,990 Q).
- Score with Stoa's rules: counts exact, measurements within 2%.
- For text questions, use a copy of the ifc-bench judge. That means abstention, then faithfulness/completeness/transparency/relevance, correct only if criteria 1-4 pass, with Haiku 5.5 as judge. Prompt source: cobbie src/baml/baml_src/answer_verifier.baml.
- Hash the Stoa cubicasa PNGs against the CubiCasa5K splits (Zenodo zip, 5.47 GB). Exclude every overlapping drawing from training, so preview accuracy stays honest.

STEP 1 (hours 1-4). Template router at $0.
- The cubicasa questions are EN+FI templates in 11 types. Match them with regex or embeddings to a target class.
- Swiss and IFC templates map to tool calls in the same way.
- Haiku 5.5 handles only questions that match no template (about $0.0005/question).
- Target: more than 95% of preview questions routed with no LLM call.

STEP 2 (hours 2-10). Train the raster detector on Verda.
- Data: CubiCasa5K SVG to YOLO-seg labels. Classes: door (opening plus leaf), window, toilet/WC seat, sink/wash basin, shower, bathtub, sauna bench, kitchen counter/stove/fridge, and room polygons with type (bedroom, bathroom, WC, sauna, kitchen, living). Start from the HF v1nz/cubicasa5k-yolo conversion for wall/door/window, and add icon and room classes from the SVG ourselves.
- Model: Ultralytics YOLO11m-seg (or YOLOv8m-seg) at imgsz 1280. Run RF-DETR-Base for comparison (Roboflow reports mAP50 74.6% on door/window/wall).
- Hardware: 1A100.22V, about 4,200 train images, about 100 epochs. Our estimate is 2-4 h, about $5-10. That figure is not from a paper.
- Optional, in parallel on 1V100 ($0.24/h): count room-label OCR tokens (MH, KH, WC, PH, SH, S, K, AVK) with PaddleOCR. Finnish plans name room types in text, and bedroom/toilet counts are what VLMs already get right (0.82-0.93 on AECV-Bench).
- Floors/storeys: count connected plan components plus floor-label OCR (1. krs / 2. krs).

STEP 3 (hours 8-14). Calibrated hybrid counting.
- Count = number of detections above a per-class threshold tuned on CubiCasa val to maximise exact-match count accuracy, not mAP.
- Detections in the uncertain band (for example 0.25-0.5) go as crops to Haiku or Sonnet 5.5 for yes/no. This is a cheap, small number of crops.
- Fall back to Claude point-placement (Point-then-Count, counting points, never the stated number) only when the detector is outside its domain: historic scans, US vector sets.
- Expected accuracy: no paper reports exact-count accuracy for a CubiCasa-trained detector, so measure it. AECV-Bench gives the baseline to beat: frontier VLMs get door/window counts exactly right on 0.30-0.43 of plans. Bedroom/toilet reach 0.82-0.93.
- Cost: YOLO inference about 20-50 ms/image on CPU, so about $0.0001/question. Compare Fable 5 at $0.077/plan and GPT-5.5 at $0.22/plan on AECV-Bench.

STEP 4 (parallel, hours 4-16). Vector and BIM slices.
- swiss_dwellings: closed polylines and hatches from DXF, areas with shapely, room names from text entities.
- ifc_models: Qto quantities or ifcopenshell geometry for slab volumes, spaces per storey.
- ifc_bench free text: a CodeAct-style IfcOpenShell agent on Sonnet 5.5 with persistent state, up to 15 code runs, and abstention. Make the answer cite the IFC class, property set or quantity behind every number to pass the 'transparency' criterion.
- Literature reference: GLM-4.7 scores 56% on the ifc-bench v2 test split. Opus 5 ranks first on the ONESTRUCTION leaderboard (number not published).

STEP 5 (hours 14-28). Verification UI and creativity.
- For every raster count, draw each counted instance as a numbered box or mask over the plan, with confidence colours. Show 'reviewed by Claude' badges on uncertain ones and click-to-toggle so a human can fix it.
- For areas, draw the polygon with its shoelace computation. For IFC, show the executed code and the entity GUIDs.
- This mirrors the P&ID 'cite the graph query' pattern that judges can check visually.

STEP 6 (hours 28-34). Full-set evaluation.
- Run a batch evaluation over the full 10 GB set's question files on the A100 (detector batch inference takes under an hour).
- Report accuracy per source and type, plus measured $/question.
- Pitch numbers: our counting exact-match against the AECV-Bench frontier baselines, and cost per question against Opus/Fable direct.

Total Verda spend: about $15-30 (1A100 roughly 6-10 h including evaluation, plus a V100 for OCR).
risks: Licence: CubiCasa5K is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and the YOLO conversion is CC BY-NC 4.0. That is fine for a hackathon demo, but a detector trained on it cannot ship commercially. Say this in the pitch, because Stoa offers a work trial.

Leakage: some Stoa cubicasa drawings may be in CubiCasa5K train/val/test. A detector trained on them will overstate preview accuracy. Deduplicate by perceptual hash, hold out the overlap, and disclose it. Never look up ground truth.

Label-convention mismatch: Stoa's ground truth (for example 'doors with leaf', 'showers+bathtubs' grouped, windows per opening or per pane, bathrooms KH/PH/PESUH/SH) may not match CubiCasa SVG classes one to one. Calibrate the class mapping and thresholds on the preview questions, not only on CubiCasa val.

Exact-match counting is unforgiving. One missed door makes the answer wrong. A detector with good mAP can still have mediocre exact-count accuracy on plans with 10-20 doors. Tune thresholds for count accuracy and use LLM review of uncertain detections.

Domain shift: the full 10 GB set holds historic scans (habs, finna, europeana, wikimedia) and US vector sets. A CubiCasa detector will degrade there, so a confidence-based fallback to Claude pointing or SAM 3 is needed. SAM 3 is untested on line-art plans.

Unverified numbers: the AECV-Bench per-field accuracies above come from our own recomputation of the repo CSVs (exact integer match per field). They differ from the abstract's '0.40-0.55' wording, which may use another definition. Training time and cost estimates for YOLO are ours, not from a paper.

IFC-Bench free-text grading depends on the judge. Scores differ by judge model (the public code defaults to the answering model or GLM-4.7, and ONESTRUCTION fixed DeepSeek-V3.2). Stoa's own text grading is unknown ('no metric'), so optimise for the rubric criteria, not one judge.
We found no papers named BlueprintQA, CAD-VQA, ArchiText or DrawingQA. Do not cite them in the pitch.

Time: 36 hours is tight for data conversion (SVG to YOLO with icons and rooms), training, calibration, the UI and a full-set evaluation. Ship the template router and vector/IFC tools first, so the score does not depend on the detector.

track: Exploiting vector structure (PDF vector paths, DXF/DWG, SVG) for symbol spotting and room/area extraction

key_findings.title: MEASURED ON PREVIEW: Swiss Dwellings DXF siblings are fully layered, so a deterministic solver already gets ~97% of Swiss questions at $0
key_findings.what: Every swiss_dwellings PDF has a same-stem DXF (65 pdf / 65 dxf / 65 png in the preview). It is written by ezdxf in metres ($INSUNITS=6) with semantic layers: ROOM_OUTLINE (closed LWPOLYLINE per room), UNIT_OUTLINE, ROOM_TEXT (name, room number like '5.11', and the area label '13.62 m²'), DOOR (one 5-vertex leaf rectangle + one ARC per door), WINDOW (3 rectangles per window), FIXTURE (48-vertex ellipses = WC bowls and basins, 69-vertex polylines = bathtubs), WALL hatches. I scored simple rules on all 2,358 Swiss preview questions (scripts in /private/tmp/claude-501/-repo/165be0a0-3c4e-47f1-97b0-ffd36f328f8d/scratchpad/vec/): room net area by number = shoelace area of the ROOM_OUTLINE that contains the number text: 256/256 within 2% (exact to 0.01 m²). Doors = count of 5-vertex DOOR polylines: 65/65 (ARC count only 37/65, double/sliding doors differ). Windows = WINDOW rectangles / 3: 65/65 (union-components only 49/65). Bathtubs = 69-vertex FIXTURE polylines: 56/56. Apartments = count of 'App. X' ROOM_TEXT labels: 65/65 (UNIT_OUTLINE count only 110/130). 'Rooms labelled X' = labels inside polygons: 662/675. Apartment net area (rooms inside unit outline, minus Balcone etc.): 106/112. Floor total net indoor area: 58/65 (needs a complete multilingual outdoor/shaft/void label list). WC + washbasin together = number of 48-vertex ellipses: 65/65, but the split WC vs basin needs one more rule (size/aspect or adjacent cistern rectangle). Showers not yet mapped.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Swiss is ~30% of preview questions (1,614 counts + 744 areas). They become exact, $0, millisecond answers, and each answer has a perfect visual proof: highlight the polygon, the label text and the shoelace formula, or the N door leaves. This is the strongest accuracy + verifiability + cost result available in this track.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: No model needed. ezdxf (MIT) + shapely (BSD). Source data: Swiss Dwellings v3.0.0, Archilyse, CC BY 4.0.

key_findings.title: MEASURED: Swiss PDFs carry the same information as vector text and styled paths
key_findings.what: PyMuPDF on site1102_bldg2242_floor10281.pdf: no OCG layers, but 150 text words in reading order ('Stanza', '5.03', '10.15', 'm²', ...), 268 vector drawings with consistent style classes (e.g. 16 gray fills 0.69 = wall hatches, 21 stroke 0.27 = door arcs). The annotation text gives 'Scala 1:100 (A3) · Misure in metri'; page is 1190.55 x 841.89 pt = A3, so 1 pt = 35.28 mm real. The printed area labels match the answers to 0.01 m².
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: If a Swiss PDF in the hidden/full set had no DXF, the answer still comes deterministically from PDF text spans (area labels) or from PDF path polygons scaled by the stated 1:100. The existing Drawing Desk PDF span-citation machinery can cite the exact label bbox.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: PyMuPDF (AGPL-3.0 or commercial licence) - fine for a non-commercial hackathon; pdfplumber/pypdfium2 are permissive alternatives.

key_findings.title: MEASURED: opening_design questions are schedule-table lookups on vector PDFs, not geometry
key_findings.what: All 64 opening_design preview questions come from 3 sheets: A-801 Door and Finish Schedules (41), A700 SCHEDULES (20), A-701 Restrooms (3). The PDFs (3024x2160 pt) have full text layers (1,885 / 2,222 / 645 words) and 5,800-23,700 vector drawings. PyMuPDF find_tables() finds 0 tables (Revit schedules are rotated and drawn as loose lines). But a regex over word tokens finds exactly 38 door ids (pattern \d{3}\.[A-Z]\d?) on A-801 = the gold answer 38; they lie on one text line, i.e. the schedule is rotated 90 degrees, so columns must be rebuilt by x-alignment.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Deterministic table reconstruction from word boxes (cluster by x for rotated tables, by y otherwise; cell borders from the vector line segments) answers the count/area/text schedule questions exactly, and the cited cells can be highlighted. An LLM (Haiku/Sonnet) only needs to map the question to a column filter, on a few KB of structured rows instead of an image.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: PyMuPDF; Camelot (MIT) lattice mode is another option for line-ruled tables.

key_findings.title: VecFormer: Point or Line? Using Line-based Representation for Panoptic Symbol Spotting in CAD Drawings (NeurIPS 2025)
key_findings.what: Transformer on a type-agnostic line-sampled representation of vector primitives, with Branch Fusion Refinement. FloorPlanCAD PQ 88.4 without layer prior (PQth 90.9, PQst 85.9) and 91.1 with layer prior; current published SOTA. Trained 500 epochs on 8x A100, batch 2/GPU. Params, training time and inference speed not reported. Uses ~15% fewer tokens than point-based input and ~8x shorter sequences than CADSpotting.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Best model if we needed learned symbol spotting on raw CAD vectors (opening_design DWG/PDF, unlayered DXF). For this dataset it is not needed: Swiss DXFs are already semantically layered and opening_design questions are schedules. Training from scratch on 8xA100 for 500 epochs does not fit 36 h, and no weights are released.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code Apache-2.0; no pretrained weights released. Paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23395

key_findings.title: SymPoint: Symbol as Points (ICLR 2024)
key_findings.what: Treats each vector primitive as a point (point cloud), Point Transformer backbone + Mask2Former-style head. 35M params, 66 ms inference per drawing (raster baselines need ~1.2 s extra to rasterize). FloorPlanCAD PQ/RQ/SQ: 79.6/89.0/89.4 at 300 epochs, 81.9/90.4/90.6 at 500, 83.3/91.1/91.4 at 1000 epochs, on 8x A100. FloorPlanCAD has 35 classes (30 thing, 5 stuff).
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Shows the cost of the learned route: long training (1000 epochs) for 83 PQ. Our rule-based layer reading beats this on Swiss data.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code: https://github.com/nicehuster/SymPoint

key_findings.title: SymPoint-V2 (SymPoint Revolutionized: Layer Feature Enhancement)
key_findings.what: Adds CAD layer features (LFE) and Position-Guided Training for faster convergence. FloorPlanCAD PQ 83.2 without prior, 90.1 with layer prior (PQth 90.8, PQst 80.8). CADSpotting notes it depends on 4 fixed primitive types and on layer info that is often missing in real drawings.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: The only top model with downloadable weights (Google Drive). Could be tried zero-shot on opening_design floor-plan sheets exported to SVG, but domain (Chinese commercial CAD, FloorPlanCAD) differs from US residential/commercial sets; expect degraded accuracy (not measured).
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code public, no licence file shown; weights on Google Drive (link in README). Env: torch 1.10 + CUDA 11.1, custom pointops op. Paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01928

key_findings.title: CADTransformer (CVPR 2022) and GAT-CADNet (CVPR 2022)
key_findings.what: CADTransformer: transformer over primitive tokens with HRNet-W48 image embedding; FloorPlanCAD PQ 68.9 (PQth 78.5, PQst 58.6); trains on a 24 GB GPU with max_prim=12000; no trained checkpoint released. GAT-CADNet: drawing as graph, symbol spotting as adjacency-matrix/subgraph prediction with relative spatial encoding; PQ 73.7, RQ 80.7, SQ 91.4; no official code (one third-party reproduction).
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Graph-on-primitives ideas are useful as features (adjacency of door leaf + arc, ellipse + cistern rectangle) for a tiny rule or GNN classifier, but the full models are dominated by VecFormer and not worth training here.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: CADTransformer: MIT, no weights. GAT-CADNet: paper https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2022/html/Zheng_GAT-CADNet_Graph_Attention_Network_for_Panoptic_Symbol_Spotting_in_CAD_CVPR_2022_paper.html; unofficial code https://github.com/Liberation-happy/GAT-CADNet

key_findings.title: CADSpotting and ArchCAD-400K / DPSS
key_findings.what: CADSpotting (arXiv 2412.07377): point-based spotting for large drawings; FloorPlanCAD PQ 88.9 with prior. ArchCAD-400K (arXiv 2503.22346): 413,062 chunks from 5,538 standardized drawings with auto line-level labels from CAD attributes; DPSS baseline fuses primitive and image features: PQ 86.2 without / 89.5 with prior on FloorPlanCAD (numbers from the VecFormer table).
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: ArchCAD-400K proves the same trick we can use: labels come for free from existing CAD attributes (layers, blocks). Swiss DXF layers are such free labels.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: No code/dataset link on the arXiv abstract page; dataset licence not stated there.

key_findings.title: 2026 follow-ups: PolarSym, TextCAD, SALI-FP
key_findings.what: PolarSym (arXiv 2608.11793, Aug 2026): polar direction/distance attention; +1.73 PQ, +1.54 RQ, +4.31 mIoU over a reproduced SymPoint-V2; absolute numbers not on abstract. TextCAD (arXiv 2607.12678, Jul 2026): fuses annotation text with primitives (Type-Attribute Correlation Encoder); numbers not on abstract. SALI-FP (arXiv 2609.25615, Sep 2026): evidence-gated multimodal floor-plan parsing and vectorization to reviewable records; ran on 11,534 production plans, 752,510 polygon objects; accuracy not on abstract.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Trend confirms Stoa's thesis: text + geometry fusion and evidence-gated, reviewable output. SALI-FP's 'constrain revisions by image evidence' matches our verifier design. None has public code.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: No code links for any of the three.

key_findings.title: FloorPlanCAD dataset
key_findings.what: 15,663 CAD drawings (Nov 2021 release) in SVG + PNG with per-primitive semantic and instance labels, 35 classes (doors, windows, sanitary fixtures, stairs, furniture, walls, etc.). Project shut down in 2022.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Only needed if training a vector spotter; licence is non-commercial.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Annotations CC BY-NC 4.0; drawings copyright not owned by authors; Google Drive downloads.

key_findings.title: CubiCasa5K SVG ground truth (cross-track: vector labels for the raster 76%)
key_findings.what: 5,000 Finnish floor plans with dense polygon SVG annotations, 80+ object categories, train/val/test lists, pretrained multi-task model weights (Google Drive). The challenge's cubicasa5k drawings come from this dataset (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Rendering SVG polygons gives exact boxes for windows, doors, WC, sinks, showers, bathtubs, saunas for a raster detector. Similarly the Swiss PNGs are rendered from the same geometry as the DXF, so DXF entities give pixel-exact detector labels for free (vector-to-raster label transfer). Overlap between public CubiCasa5K splits and challenge drawings must be handled honestly (hold-out) to avoid leakage claims.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code + weights public; dataset on Zenodo record 2613548.

key_findings.title: DWG to DXF: LibreDWG 0.13.4/0.14 vs ODA File Converter
key_findings.what: LibreDWG (GNU, GPL-3.0-or-later): manual v0.13.4 (17 Mar 2026) says it reads all DWG formats r1.2-r2018 'for 99%'; dwg2dxf writes DXF R13-R2018 (--as=rNNNN, --minimal); still labelled beta; AutoCAD fails to import some of its DXFs; Homebrew ships libredwg 0.14. ODA File Converter: free download but ODA FAQ says non-members may use it for non-commercial applications only; packaged as unfree; ezdxf has an odafc add-on that calls it.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: opening_design has 20 DWGs and 1 DXF in preview (no preview questions point at DWG). Use LibreDWG dwg2dxf as the open path (hackathon is non-commercial, GPL is fine as a separate CLI), with ODA as a fallback for files LibreDWG mangles; ezdxf recover mode to read the result. Not tested on our DWGs yet.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: LibreDWG GPL-3.0 (https://github.com/LibreDWG/libredwg). ODA: https://www.opendesign.com/faq/question/what-are-oda-viewer-and-oda-file-converter

key_findings.title: OCR with positions for room labels: PaddleOCR 3.7 (PP-OCRv6), docTR, Surya 2.5, Florence-2
key_findings.what: PaddleOCR 3.7.0 (Jun 2026, Apache-2.0): PP-OCRv6 tiny/small/medium = 1.5M/7.7M/34.5M params, 50 languages in one model; PP-OCRv5 multilingual recognizer ~2M params, 109 languages; per-character boxes since 3.2; CPU/ONNX/OpenVINO. docTR (Apache-2.0): DBNet/LinkNet/FAST detection + CRNN/PARSeq etc., word-level boxes in a Page-Block-Line-Word tree. Surya 2.5 (689M params): code Apache-2.0, weights modified OpenRAIL-M (free under $5M revenue); 90+ languages; block-level polygons only; 4.5 pages/s at 192 DPI on H100. Florence-2-large (0.77B, MIT): <OCR_WITH_REGION> returns quad boxes + text.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Not needed for Swiss or opening_design (text layers exist). Needed for raster CubiCasa (Finnish room codes KH, MH, WC, S, PH) and scanned sets: PaddleOCR PP-OCRv6 small on CPU is the cheapest word-box OCR; matching a label to a room = point-in-polygon of the OCR box centre against segmented room polygons.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: PaddleOCR Apache-2.0; docTR https://github.com/mindee/doctr Apache-2.0; Surya https://github.com/datalab-to/surya; Florence-2 https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Florence-2-large MIT

concrete_recipe:
Answer to the key question: YES for Swiss Dwellings (measured), and YES for the opening_design questions that exist (they are schedule lookups on text-layer PDFs). No GPU and no LLM call are needed for the answer itself.

Phase 1 (hours 0-5): Swiss DXF solver, CPU only.
1. For a swiss_dwellings PDF, open the same-stem .dxf with ezdxf. Build rooms = closed LWPOLYLINE on ROOM_OUTLINE (shapely Polygon, buffer(0)). Assign ROOM_TEXT entities by point-in-polygon (use align_point when halign/valign are set). Each room gets name, number, printed area.
2. Rules (preview score in brackets): room area = polygon.area in m2 [256/256]; also cross-check against the printed 'xx.xx m²' label and flag any disagreement > 0.5%. Doors = number of 5-vertex DOOR polylines [65/65]. Windows = WINDOW rectangles / 3; better, group 3 parallel rectangles per opening [65/65]. Bathtubs = 69-vertex FIXTURE polylines [56/56]. Apartments = number of 'App. X' / 'Wohnung' / 'Appartement' labels [65/65]. Rooms labelled X = labels inside polygons, case-insensitive [662/675, fix the misses]. Apartment net area = rooms whose representative point is inside the UNIT_OUTLINE that holds the 'App. X' label, minus outdoor labels [106/112]. Floor net area = numbered rooms minus outdoor, shaft and void labels in DE/FR/IT/EN [58/65; finish the label list].
3. Still open: split 48-vertex ellipses into WC vs washbasin (sum is 65/65). Fit a 3-feature rule (major axis, minor axis, a 4-vertex cistern rectangle touching the ellipse) on the preview, then check it on held-out floors. Map showers the same way (likely a 4-vertex rectangle with 2-point diagonals).
4. Question routing: regex templates in 4 languages (EN/DE/FR/IT) cover all 10 Swiss templates. Use Haiku only as fallback to map an unseen phrasing to a template (~300 tokens, ~$0.0003).
5. Visual proof: render the PDF page, overlay the chosen polygons or entities in a color, list the vertices and the shoelace sum, and show the printed label beside the computed area. A human checks it in seconds.
Expected: >=97% on Swiss questions now, ~99% after steps 3-4. Cost: $0, <100 ms per question.

Phase 2 (hours 5-10): opening_design schedules.
1. PyMuPDF words with boxes. Detect schedule tables by header tokens (DOOR SCHEDULE, ROOM FINISH SCHEDULE, WINDOW). Rebuild rows and columns by clustering word boxes along the reading axis; detect 90-degree rotation from word direction (dir field in get_text('dict')). Use vector line segments as cell borders where present.
2. Emit a typed table (JSON) with a bbox per cell. Sonnet or Haiku writes a filter or aggregation over the JSON (not over the image); Python runs it; the UI highlights the counted cells. Preview check: 38 door ids on A-801 = gold 38.
3. A-701 fixture counts (3 questions): count WATER CLOSET / LAVATORY tags or repeated vector block geometry inside the named enlarged-plan viewport (match identical path signatures by hashing the normalized path list). Cost ~$0.001-0.005 per question with Haiku or Sonnet on a small text payload.

Phase 3 (hours 10-14): DWG and general vector PDFs.
1. Install LibreDWG dwg2dxf (0.13.4/0.14, GPL-3.0) in a uv tool or a container, not in the shared machine config. Convert with dwg2dxf --as=r2018. Read with ezdxf.recover. Keep ODA File Converter as a manual fallback only (non-commercial use only).
2. Generic room extraction for unlayered vector PDFs/DXFs: collect wall-like strokes (by line width or layer name), snap endpoints (1-2 cm tolerance), close door gaps by joining the door leaf chord, then shapely.polygonize. Assign room labels by point-in-polygon of text spans. Scale from the title block ('1:100') or a dimension string. Report the polygon on the page as proof.

Phase 4, optional Verda job (hours 14-24), aimed at the raster 76%, not at vector data.
1. Make free detector labels: Swiss PNGs are rendered from the same geometry as the DXF, so map DOOR/WINDOW/FIXTURE entities to PNG boxes (affine from the DXF extents to the PNG frame). Add CubiCasa5K SVG polygons (windows, doors, WC, sinks, showers, bathtubs, sauna stove) rasterized to boxes.
2. Train an Apache-licensed detector (RT-DETRv2 or D-FINE; avoid AGPL Ultralytics if licence matters) on 1x A100 80 GB ($2.37/h) for 3-5 h, about $10. Hold out every challenge drawing from training to avoid leakage. Accuracy is not measured; set a target of >=90% exact counts on held-out CubiCasa floors before switching the raster path from Claude points to the detector.
3. Do NOT train VecFormer/SymPoint: published runs use 8x A100 for 500-1000 epochs, and no question in the preview needs learned vector spotting.

Budget: Swiss + opening_design answers at $0-0.005 per question. Total compute for this track: under $15 of Verda credit (optional Phase 4 only).
risks: The full 10 GB set may have Swiss PDFs without a DXF sibling, or different layer names. Mitigation: a PDF-only route from text spans (printed 'xx.xx m²' labels) and styled vector paths at the stated 1:100 A3 scale. It is built on the same rules and still deterministic.

The rules were fit on 65 Swiss preview floors (e.g. 'windows = rectangles / 3', 'doors = 5-vertex polylines'). They can break on special openings: sliding doors, bay or corner windows, double doors drawn differently. Validate on a held-out slice of the full set before you trust 100%. Keep the printed label vs polygon area cross-check as a self-test.
WC vs washbasin split and shower mapping are not solved yet. Only their sum is exact (65/65).
Label lists for outdoor, shaft and void rooms in DE/FR/IT/EN decide the floor net area questions (58/65 now). A missed synonym silently changes the sum.

Exploiting a DXF sibling to answer a question that points at the PDF can look like 'reading the answer key'. Present it as a legitimate multi-format ingest: the README says that files with the same name are the same drawing in another format. Also show that the PDF-only route agrees.

opening_design schedules are rotated and not line-ruled for PyMuPDF find_tables (0 tables found). Column reconstruction from word boxes can misalign merged or multi-line cells (e.g. '5'-10 3/8"'). Text answers are free-form, so the scoring is unclear.

LibreDWG is beta: it reads r1.2-r2018 'for 99%', and some of its DXFs fail in AutoCAD. Not yet tested on the 20 opening_design DWGs. ODA File Converter is non-commercial only for non-members. That is fine for the hackathon but not for a product.

Learned vector spotters (VecFormer, SymPoint-V2, CADSpotting) were trained on FloorPlanCAD (CC BY-NC, Chinese CAD conventions) on 8x A100 for 500-1000 epochs. Zero-shot transfer to US or Swiss drawings is unmeasured. SymPoint-V2 shows no licence file, and VecFormer has no released weights.

Licences: PyMuPDF is AGPL, Ultralytics YOLO is AGPL, Surya weights are restricted above $5M revenue, and CubiCasa5K is CC BY-NC-SA. Acceptable for a non-commercial hackathon demo, but name them if Stoa asks about productization.
CubiCasa5K public splits may contain the challenge drawings. If you train on them without holding out the challenge drawings, the result is contaminated.

track: Low-cost, verifiable agentic architectures for drawing QA: routers and cascades, deterministic tool calling, verifiers vs self-consistency, abstention, caching and batch, distillation of tool traces, evidence UIs, and cost per question

key_findings.title: AECV-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Models on Architectural and Engineering Drawings Understanding
key_findings.what: Kondratenko et al., Jan 2026. Counting on 120 floor plans (doors, windows, bedrooms, toilets) plus 192 document QA pairs. Door and window counting by frontier multimodal models 'remains unsolved (often 0.40-0.55 accuracy)'. OCR and text QA reach up to 0.95. The authors recommend domain representations and tool workflows with a human in the loop.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This is the key result for our biggest gap. If Claude places points directly on raster plans, expect about 40-55% exact counts on doors and windows. Read text with OCR or a VLM (0.95). Count symbols with a trained detector. Use Claude only to adjudicate.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: No code or data link on the abstract page

key_findings.title: CubiCasa5K dataset and multi-task model
key_findings.what: 5,000 Finnish floor plans with polygon SVG annotations in more than 80 categories. Split is 4200 train / 400 val / 400 test (per secondary sources). Icon classes include Window, Door, Closet, Toilet, Sink, Sauna Bench, Bathtub and Fireplace. A pretrained multi-task segmentation model (Raster-to-Vector derived, PyTorch) is in the repo. A later paper (2408.01526) reports the original baseline IoU as about 0.53 for doors and 0.66 for windows.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This is the source of the cubicasa5k questions (76% of the preview are counts). The SVG labels give free supervision to train a detector on Verda for the exact icons asked about (toilets, sinks, showers and baths, saunas, doors, windows). Check for overlap between the challenge images and the CubiCasa train split before you claim accuracy.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code and pretrained weights (Google Drive link in README). Licence CC BY-NC 4.0, so non-commercial only.

key_findings.title: cubicassa5k-coco (Hugging Face dataset)
key_findings.what: CubiCasa5K converted to COCO instance segmentation as Parquet: 4,228 train / 748 valid images, 270k polygons. Only 8 classes: wall, door, window, room, bathroom, kitchen, bed, stairs. Heavy class imbalance.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Gives a ready door and window detector or segmenter dataset without parsing SVG. It does NOT have toilet, sink, shower, bathtub or sauna, so parse the original SVG for those icon classes.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Dataset public. 'cubicasa5k-research-license', which inherits the upstream CC BY-NC terms.

key_findings.title: RF-DETR (Roboflow, ICLR 2026)
key_findings.what: Real-time DETR detector and segmenter. Detection Nano/Small/Medium/Large: 48.4/53.0/54.7/56.5 COCO AP at 2.3/3.5/4.4/6.8 ms on T4 (TensorRT FP16). Segmentation sizes 40.3-49.9 AP. About 30-34M params. A Roboflow Universe CubiCasa model (door, window, wall) reports mAP@50 74.6%.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: An Apache-2.0 alternative to Ultralytics YOLO (AGPL-3.0). It fine-tunes on CubiCasa icons in a few GPU hours. Inference costs effectively $0 per drawing, and each detection is a box a human can check.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code and weights. Apache 2.0 for N/S/M/L and all segmentation sizes. PML 1.0 for XL/2XL.

key_findings.title: Grounding DINO zero-shot on CubiCasa (community repo heypaprika/gdino)
key_findings.what: Zero-shot mAP@0.5 is about 0.0 on 10 CubiCasa classes (400 test plans). The prompt '{class} symbol' raises toilet recall from 6% to 21% and sink from 6% to 19%. Thin linear symbols (doors, windows) stay at about 0%.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Open-vocabulary detectors and counters (Grounding DINO, CountGD) do not transfer to architectural symbols. A supervised detector trained on CubiCasa labels is required. Do not spend hackathon hours on zero-shot CV.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code public on GitHub. Licence not checked.

key_findings.title: Set-of-Mark Prompting (SoM)
key_findings.what: Yang et al. 2023 (Microsoft). Overlay numbered marks, masks or boxes from a segmenter on the image. The multimodal LLM then refers to marks by ID. Zero-shot GPT-4V with SoM beat fully fine-tuned referring-expression models on RefCOCOg.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This is the escalation pattern. The detector proposes numbered candidates. Claude only accepts or rejects mark IDs and may add missed points, so its output stays grounded and checkable, and it needs far fewer output tokens than free pointing. The same numbered marks are the evidence in the UI.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code at github.com/microsoft/SoM

key_findings.title: Getting to the Point: Pointing Improves LVLMs at Counting
key_findings.what: Alghisi et al., Mar 2026. Point-then-Count (point at each instance, then count the points) gives the highest accuracy among the methods they tested. Predicted points are correctly placed in more than 94% of cases (F1), and the method generalizes better out of distribution. The abstract gives no headline accuracy delta.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Supports our existing count = len(points) design as the right fallback for a VLM, and as the right evidence format. It is still worse than a trained detector on domain symbols (see AECV-Bench).
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: No code link. Paper CC BY 4.0.

key_findings.title: RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data
key_findings.what: Ong et al. (LMSYS), ICLR 2025. Strong/weak routers (matrix factorization, BERT, causal LLM, similarity-weighted Elo) are trained on preference data. The README reports up to 85% cost reduction while keeping 95% of GPT-4 quality on MT-Bench, and more than 40% cheaper than commercial routers.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: A learned router is overkill here. Our routing signal is mostly deterministic: file type, question template and tool confidence. Its useful lesson is to calibrate the threshold so a target fraction goes to the strong model.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code and router weights on HF (routellm org). Apache-2.0.

key_findings.title: FrugalGPT
key_findings.what: Chen, Zaharia, Zou 2023. An LLM cascade with a learned answer scorer. It matches GPT-4 with up to 98% cost reduction, or gives +4% accuracy at equal cost.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This is the canonical cheap-first cascade with a scorer. In our setting the scorer can be deterministic (detector confidence, agreement with OCR, geometry checks) instead of a learned model.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Not stated on the abstract page

key_findings.title: A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs (cascade routing)
key_findings.what: Dekoninck, Baader, Vechev (ETH), 2024, revised Oct 2026. Proves optimal cascading and routing strategies and unifies them as 'cascade routing', which beats both. Main finding: the accuracy of the quality estimator is the key factor in whether model selection works.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Spend the engineering effort on the confidence signal (calibrated on the 7,990 preview questions), not on adding more models.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Not stated on the abstract page

key_findings.title: Is Escalation Worth It? On the Depth of LLM Cascades
key_findings.what: Bouchard, May/Oct 2026. Over an 8-model pool and 5 benchmarks, 2-model cascades add 2.1-8.2 points of mean accuracy over the best single model. Deeper cascades give no gain in 118 of 135 comparisons (at most +0.43 points). Depth helps only when the deferral score tracks the current model's own errors, not shared query difficulty.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Build exactly two tiers: cheap deterministic CV/tools, then Opus adjudication. A middle Sonnet or Haiku vision tier is unlikely to pay off.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Not stated

key_findings.title: Cost-Saving LLM Cascades with Early Abstention
key_findings.what: Zellinger, Liu, Thomson 2025. Small and large models make correlated mistakes, so the cheap model may abstain early. Across 6 benchmarks: overall loss -2.2%, cost -13%, error -5%, abstention +4.1%.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Supports a 'needs review' outcome when the cheap tier is unsure and the question type is known to defeat Claude too (for example dense door counts). Show the uncertain marks instead of paying Opus to guess.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Not stated

key_findings.title: Dynamic Model Routing and Cascading for Efficient LLM Inference: A Survey
key_findings.what: Moslem and Kelleher, TMLR 2026. Survey of routing by difficulty, preference, clustering, uncertainty, RL, multimodality and cascades. It describes a common 3-stage pipeline: pre-router, quality estimator, escalation policy.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Good citation for the pitch. Our design is an instance of this pipeline with a deterministic pre-router (file type and question template).
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: N/A (survey)

key_findings.title: AutoMix: Automatically Mixing Language Models
key_findings.what: Aggarwal, Madaan et al., NeurIPS 2024. Few-shot self-verification by the small model plus a POMDP router to handle noisy verification. More than 50% compute cost reduction at comparable performance.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Self-verification is noisy. Prefer external, deterministic verification (point inside room polygon, OCR label agreement, area recompute) over asking the model whether it is sure.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: No repo linked on the abstract page. Paper CC BY 4.0.

key_findings.title: Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
key_findings.what: Brown et al. 2024. Coverage rises log-linearly with the number of samples. With an automatic verifier this becomes accuracy (SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% at 250 samples). Without one, majority voting and reward models plateau after a few hundred samples.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Self-consistency (vote over N Claude samples) costs N times as much and plateaus. Correlated VLM counting errors make voting weak. Spend the budget on deterministic verifiers and on agreement between different signal types (detector vs OCR vs VLM).
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Not stated on the abstract page

key_findings.title: Mitigating LLM Hallucinations via Conformal Abstention
key_findings.what: Abbasi Yadkori et al. (DeepMind) 2024. Conformal prediction on self-consistency similarity scores decides when to abstain, with a theoretical bound on the error rate. Less conservative than log-prob baselines on long answers.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Use split-conformal calibration on the preview set to set the escalate and abstain thresholds for a stated target error, for example at most 5% wrong among answered counts. This also gives a clean slide for the accuracy criterion.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Not stated

key_findings.title: Program of Thoughts Prompting
key_findings.what: Chen et al., TMLR 2023. The LLM writes code and an interpreter does the arithmetic. About +12% on average over chain-of-thought across math and financial QA. SOTA on math datasets with self-consistency.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Supports our design: area, volume and length always come from executed tools (IFC Qto, DXF polylines, shoelace on detected polygons), never from model arithmetic. The 2% tolerance makes model arithmetic a needless risk.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code at github.com/wenhuchen/Program-of-Thoughts

key_findings.title: ViperGPT: Visual Inference via Python Execution
key_findings.what: Surís, Menon, Vondrick 2023. An LLM writes Python that composes vision modules through an API. Interpretable, and needs no training.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Precedent for 'Claude writes a short program over our drawing API' (detections, OCR spans, room polygons). The executed program is itself an evidence trail.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Project site viper.cs.columbia.edu. No repo on the abstract page.

key_findings.title: Visual Program Distillation (VPD)
key_findings.what: Hu et al., CVPR 2024 Oral. Sample several tool-calling programs from an LLM, execute them, keep a verified-correct one, turn it into a rationale and fine-tune a VLM (PaLI-X). SOTA claimed on TallyQA (counting), MMBench, OK-VQA and POPE, and the VLM answers in a single forward pass.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This is the recipe for distilling Opus tool traces. Keep only traces whose answer matches ground truth (rejection sampling), then SFT a small open model. Latency and cost drop to one forward pass.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: No official code linked. Paper CC BY 4.0.

key_findings.title: Distilling LLM Agent into Small Models with Retrieval and Code Tools (Agent Distillation)
key_findings.what: Kang et al., NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight. Distills full ReAct/code-tool trajectories from a Qwen2.5-32B teacher (about 2k trajectories) into 0.5B/1.5B/3B students with TRL SFT. Students match CoT-distilled models one size up (0.5B ~ 1.5B, 3B ~ 7B). Adds 'first-thought prefix' and self-consistent action generation.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: A small, fast distillation target for the hackathon: a 1.5B-3B text-only planner that maps a question in any of about 30 languages to a tool program, for example count(class='toilet', drawing=...). It runs on a V100 and gives a credible 'trained on Verda' story.

key_findings.title: Claude vision token cost, coordinates, caching and batch (official docs)
key_findings.what: Image tokens = ceil(w/28) x ceil(h/28). Claude 4.7+ high-res tier: long edge up to 2,576 px and at most 4,784 tokens. Docs: a 1000x1000 image is 1,296 tokens, about $5.18 per 1,000 images on Opus 5.5. Ask for absolute pixel coordinates (not 0-1000). Pre-resize so coordinates map 1:1. Crop for small targets. PDFs are rasterized server-side, so coordinates do not map back: rasterize yourself. Prices per MTok: Opus 5.5 $4 in / $20 out, cache read $0.20 (0.05x), 5-minute cache write $5. Sonnet 5.5 $2/$10. Haiku 5.5 $0.10/$0.50, cache read $0.01. Batch API -50% on input and output, stacks with caching. Minimum cacheable prefix 286 tokens.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: A full-resolution plan costs about $0.019 of input on Opus 5.5 and about $0.0005 on Haiku 5.5. Put all questions for one drawing behind one cached image prefix, or answer them in one call, and run evaluation through Batch.

key_findings.title: Fostering Appropriate Reliance on LLMs: The Role of Explanations, Sources, and Inconsistencies (CHI 2025)
key_findings.what: Kim et al. Think-aloud study (n=16) plus a pre-registered experiment (N=308). Explanations increase reliance on both correct AND incorrect answers. Sources increase appropriate reliance and decrease overreliance on wrong answers. Visible inconsistencies reduce overreliance.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: UI rule: lead with checkable evidence (marks on the drawing, IFC entity IDs, OCR spans), not prose rationale. When signals disagree (detector says 7, OCR labels say 6), show the disagreement. It helps the human catch errors.

key_findings.title: Effects of LLM-based Search on Decision Making: Speed, Accuracy, and Overreliance (CHI 2025)
key_findings.what: Spatharioti, Rothschild, Goldstein, Hofman. LLM search halved time-on-task with similar accuracy when the model was right, but users overrelied when it was wrong. The extracted text suggests roughly 50% less overreliance, but this figure is not verified from clean text.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Color each mark and each answer by confidence (detector score, agreement). The reviewer then checks only the red marks, so verification takes seconds instead of a full recount.

key_findings.title: PaperTrail: claim-evidence interface (CHI 2026) and Citations and Trust in LLM Answers (AAAI 2025)
key_findings.what: PaperTrail (within-subjects study, 26 researchers) maps each claim to evidence and shows supported, unsupported and omitted claims. Every mark and quote passes the deterministic verifier, and a 'verified by tool' badge separates computed answers from model judgements. key_findings.title: When Should a Network Emit Geometry, and When Should It Detect It? (floorplan vectorization)
key_findings.what: He Zhang, Aug 2026. On CubiCasa5K, detection (heatmaps to graph) beats autoregressive emission on walls (+2.7 / +5.1 F1). Deterministic fusion of both raises wall F1 by 7 points. Releases corrected CubiCasa annotations, the ResPlan-FP benchmark (16,998 plans, CC BY 4.0) and an 'edit-cost' metric (how much human correction a draft needs).
