concrete_recipe:
GOAL: route about 85-90% of questions to $0 deterministic tools with machine-checked evidence. Escalate the rest to Opus 5.5 as an adjudicator over numbered candidate marks, not as a free counter. Abstain with marked uncertainty when the signals still disagree. All per-question costs below are estimates from official prices and published throughput. Accuracy numbers are targets to measure, not results.

STEP 0 (hours 0-2): baseline harness. Score the 7,990 preview questions per (dataset, question template) with the official rules: exact for counts, 2% for area, length and volume. Add two baselines that cost nothing: (a) the mode answer per template, which is probably high for floors, saunas and kitchens; (b) the current Claude point-placing loop on about 300 sampled questions through the Batch API (about $5-15). This gives the real gap per template. Check whether the preview cubicasa images are in the CubiCasa5K train/val/test lists (match by image hash). Never look up their SVG at inference time.

STEP 1 (hours 1-4): deterministic router and question parser. Route by file type first: IFC goes to ifcopenshell/Qto, DXF to blocks, layers and polylines, vector PDF to text spans plus vector paths, PNG/JPG to the raster pipeline. Parse questions with regex for the EN/FI template pairs (they are templated). Fall back to Haiku 5.5 with structured output and a cached system prompt (about 3k tokens) that maps any of about 30 languages to {source, op: count|area|volume|length|lookup, class, filters, storey, unit}. Cost about $0.0002-0.0004 per question. Optional Verda bonus: distill this parser into Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. Use about 5-10k Haiku-labelled questions from the full set, keep only parses whose tool result matches ground truth, and train with TRL SFT on 1xA100 for about 1 h (about $3), following the Agent Distillation and VPD pattern.

STEP 2 (hours 2-14, on Verda): raster CV inventory for CubiCasa-style plans.
(a) Build labels. Parse the CubiCasa5K SVGs (train split only; hold out val) into COCO boxes and masks for: door, window, toilet, sink, shower, bathtub, sauna bench, plus room polygons with room type. Start from the HF cubicassa5k-coco set for door and window.
(b) Train RF-DETR-Seg Medium or Large (Apache-2.0) at 1024-1280 px on 1xA100 80GB ($2.37/h). Plan 3-6 h, about $7-15 with margin. Training time is not reported for this dataset, so set --hours 8 and watch validation mAP. Fallback: the pretrained CubiCasa multi-task model from the repo, which gives icon and room segmentation and needs no training.
(c) Run PaddleOCR (PP-OCRv6 small) on every plan. Count room-type labels (MH, KH/PH/PESUH/SH, WC, S/SAUNA, K/KEITTIÖ/KT) and assign each label to a room polygon.
(d) Precompute one inventory JSON per drawing: detections with score, box and mask; OCR spans; rooms; storeys (count the separate plan regions or floor-name labels). This is computed once per drawing and serves about 20 questions. GPU cost about $0.000005 per drawing on V100, effectively $0 per question.

STEP 3 (hours 10-18): confidence and the cascade (two tiers only).
Answer = lookup in the inventory. Confidence features per question: number of detections in the uncertain score band (for example 0.3-0.6), agreement between independent signals (fixture detections vs OCR room labels: toilets vs WC/KH rooms, bedrooms by OCR vs room-type segmentation), and template difficulty.
Calibrate with split conformal or a simple threshold search on half the preview set for a target error rate on accepted answers (for example 5%). Report coverage and accuracy on the other half.
Escalate to Opus 5.5 with Set-of-Mark: one image pre-resized to at most 2576 px long edge (at most 4,784 tokens), candidates drawn as numbered boxes, crops of the uncertain marks. Ask for structured output {accept:[ids], reject:[ids], add:[[x,y]...], answer}. Pixel coordinates must map 1:1. The deterministic verifier checks that added points land on ink and inside the plan, that the count equals accepted + added, and that every accepted ID exists.
Cost per escalation, about 10k input / 800 output tokens: about $0.056 standard, about $0.03 with Batch. Put the system prompt and the drawing image first with cache_control so that later questions on the same drawing read the image at $0.20/MTok.
If the verifier fails, or Opus disagrees with both CV signals, return 'needs review' with the disputed marks in red (abstention).

STEP 4 (in parallel, hours 4-20): vector and BIM paths are already tool-based. Add a polygon-area tool (shoelace on DXF, IFC or detected room polygons, with the scale from a DXF unit or a scale-bar OCR) so that all area, volume and length answers come from executed code (PoT). Swiss Dwellings: use the DXF/PDF geometry for room-type counts and areas at $0. Use Claude only for free-text ifc_bench and opening_design schedule lookups, via the existing span-citing loop, with Sonnet 5.5 or Opus at low effort.

STEP 5 (hours 14-30): evidence UI. For every answer show: (1) the drawing with numbered marks or highlighted polygons, colored by confidence (green tool-verified, amber model-accepted, red disputed); (2) a side list 'counted 7 = marks 1-7', where clicking a mark toggles it and recomputes the answer live (edit-cost); (3) the provenance chain as chips: router decision, tool call, tool output, verifier checks passed, cost in $ and tokens for this answer, tier used; (4) for areas: the polygon, its vertex list, the formula and the scale source; (5) disagreements between signals shown explicitly. Lead with evidence, not prose explanations (CHI 2025 findings).

STEP 6 (hours 28-34): final evaluation on the full preview, run through the Batch API for the escalated part. Report per-template accuracy, coverage, escalation rate and dollars per 1,000 questions. Show the cost and accuracy frontier against the 'Opus does everything' baseline.

COST PER QUESTION (estimates; full-res plan about 4.8k image tokens, about 3k system/tool tokens):
- Claude Opus 5.5 agentic loop with images, 3 turns (about 31k input / 3.3k output cumulative): about $0.19 uncached, about $0.10-0.12 with prompt caching, about $0.05-0.06 with Batch plus caching.
- Opus 5.5 single shot (image + question, about 8k in / 600 out): about $0.044, $0.022 with Batch.
- One Opus call that answers all ~20 questions of a drawing at once: about $0.15 per drawing, about $0.008 per question.
- Haiku 5.5 single shot: about $0.0011, $0.0006 with Batch. Haiku 3-turn loop: about $0.005.
- Local Qwen2.5-VL-7B (vLLM) on 1xA100 at $2.37/h: about $0.0009 per question at the published 0.7 QPS for 1680x2240 document images, about $0.0002 at 3 QPS with max_pixels capped near 1 MP. On 1xV100 at $0.24/h the throughput is not reported; with fp16 only and no FlashAttention-2, a guess of 3-5x slower gives about $0.0003-0.0005. Idle VM time dominates at hackathon scale.
- Pure CV + OCR + rules: about $0.000005 per drawing on GPU (CPU also works), effectively $0 per question once amortized over about 20 questions per drawing.
- Blended cascade, assuming 10-15% escalation: about $0.004-0.008 per question, about $0.002-0.004 with Batch. That is about 25-50x cheaper than Opus per question.

EXPECTED ACCURACY: not reported for this exact setup, so measure it. Reference points: frontier VLMs score about 0.40-0.55 exact on door and window counts (AECV-Bench). OCR and text tasks reach up to 0.95. The CubiCasa baseline segmentation IoU is about 0.53 for doors and 0.66 for windows. DoorDet reports about 7.8 doors per plan, so an exact door count needs almost every instance right. Realistic targets: OCR-label templates (bedrooms, bathrooms, WC, saunas, kitchens) and fixtures (toilets, sinks) at 80-90%+; doors and windows at 60-75% after adjudication; IFC/DXF quantities at more than 90% where the tool resolves the right entity.

VERDA USE: RF-DETR training on 1xA100 (about $10-20), optional parser distillation on 1xA100 (about $3), batch OCR and detection inventory on 1xV100 ($0.24/h). Total well under $50.
risks: Train/test leakage: the CubiCasa5K SVG labels are public. If preview or hidden drawings are CubiCasa images, a detector trained on all 5,000 plans inflates accuracy, and reading their SVG at inference would be cheating. Hash-match the challenge images against the splits, train only on images not in the evaluation set, and say this openly to the judges.

Label semantics do not match: CubiCasa 'Door' polygons may not equal 'doors with a leaf'. Garage openings, French doors and glazed openings are handled differently (AECV-Bench counting rules). Shower vs bathtub, and 'separate WC room' vs a WC fixture, need rules tuned on preview answers.

Licences: CubiCasa5K is CC BY-NC 4.0 (fine for the hackathon, not for Stoa production use without permission). Ultralytics YOLO is AGPL-3.0, so prefer RF-DETR N/S/M/L (Apache-2.0). Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B are Apache-2.0. RF-DETR XL/2XL are PML 1.0.

Detector training time and resolution: floor-plan symbols are small and thin. At 512-576 px, doors and windows may vanish, while 1024+ px needs more VRAM and time. Budget a fallback to the pretrained CubiCasa multi-task model if RF-DETR is not converged by about hour 14.

Calibration overfitting: thresholds tuned on 320 preview drawings (about 4k cubicasa questions, highly correlated within a drawing) can overstate coverage. Split by drawing, not by question, when you calibrate and report.

Escalation may not help: correlated errors (Zellinger 2025; Bouchard 2026) mean Opus may fail on the same dense door clusters that fool the detector. Measure Opus adjudication accuracy on escalated cases. If it adds little, abstain instead of paying.

Coordinate mismatch: Claude coordinates refer to the resized image, and PDFs are rasterized server-side. Always rasterize yourself, pre-resize to the high-res tier limits, and set transformations.oversized_image='error' so marks cannot drift silently.

Opus 5.5 API changes: forced tool_choice returns a 400, thinking cannot be disabled, and the default effort is medium. Use tool_choice auto with strict tools or structured outputs, and set effort explicitly (low for adjudication). Caches are model-scoped, so a cascade loses cache reuse across models.

Haiku 5.5 is so cheap (about $0.001 per question) that a local 7B VLM gives almost no cost advantage for a demo. Justify Verda training by accuracy (a domain detector) and offline or privacy use, not by inference cost alone.

OCR on Finnish abbreviations: short labels (S, K, MH) collide with dimension text and other annotations. Restrict OCR label matching to text inside room polygons and to a whitelist, and show each counted label box so errors are visible.

Scope over 36 hours: CV training, calibration, the UI and the IFC/DXF paths at once is tight. If time runs out, cut parser distillation first, then conformal calibration (use a simple threshold), never the evidence UI.

track: Multilingual question-to-structured-query parsing (semantic parsing to a DSL), at low cost

key_findings.title: Local measurement: the preview question set is a closed template set, and 95.0% of questions on unseen drawings match a template seen elsewhere
key_findings.what: I analysed questions.jsonl (7,990 questions). I replaced quoted strings with <Q> and numbers with <N>, which gives 465 distinct question signatures. cubicasa5k has only 24 signatures (12 intents x EN/FI). swiss_dwellings has about 73 (EN/DE/FR/IT) and ifc_models about 65 (EN/ET/DA/DE). A 5-fold split by drawing measured how many held-out questions have a signature seen in the training drawings: cubicasa5k 100%, swiss_dwellings 99.4%, ifc_models 92.0%, ifc_bench 3.2%, opening_design 0%, all 95.0%. The slots are verbatim strings from the drawing, in the drawing's language: an Italian drawing gets 'Stanza' in both the EN question and the IT question. They are not translated. 1,395 of 2,335 (path, answer) groups are exact EN plus local-language pairs. Median question length is 69 characters.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: For about 95% of questions, a parser does not need ML. Slot extraction plus an exact template lookup costs $0 and is deterministic. Only the free-form families (ifc_bench, opening_design, about 4% of the preview) and unseen templates or languages in the hidden 120k set need a learned model or an LLM. The EN/local pairing lets us label every local-language template automatically from about 45 hand-labelled EN templates.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Analysis script was run inline. It is not saved.

key_findings.title: When Do LLMs Replace Fine-Tuned NLU? A Decision Framework for Intent Detection in Production Conversational Systems (Rodrigues, Vas)
key_findings.what: The paper compares fine-tuned RoBERTa with Claude Haiku zero-shot. ATIS accuracy: RoBERTa 95.9 vs Haiku 84.1 (p<0.001). CLINC150: 89.1 vs 88.5 (statistical tie). The LLM wins on out-of-scope recall (85.6 vs 58.1), on ASR noise at 0 dB (92.5 vs 80.0) and on new intents without retraining (~94% vs 0%). The fine-tuned encoder is about three orders of magnitude cheaper and faster. Rule from the paper: with abundant labels and a stable intent set, use the encoder. When out-of-scope detection matters or the schema changes, use a schema-prompted LLM.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This supports a cascade. A trained encoder or a lookup handles the stable template intents. A Haiku fallback handles the out-of-scope and unseen questions, where the encoder is weak.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: No code link on the arXiv page. Paper is a 6-page preprint.

key_findings.title: MASSIVE: A 1M-Example Multilingual NLU Dataset with 51 Typologically-Diverse Languages (FitzGerald et al.)
key_findings.what: Parallel intent plus slot dataset: 1M utterances, 51 languages, 60 intents, 55 slots. Full-training exact-match (intent and all slots correct), as reported in a follow-up table: mT5 text-to-text 66.6 average (73.4 high, 58.3 low locale), mT5 encoder 65.9, XLM-R 63.7. Zero-shot cross-lingual exact match is 25-37 points worse than full-data training. A follow-up raised exact match from 68.3 to 78.5 with machine-translated and synthetic data.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Do not depend on zero-shot cross-lingual transfer for the ~30 languages. Generate training pairs in each target language: translate the templates with Haiku, then fill the slots. Our template language is much narrower than MASSIVE's open utterances, so exact match should be much higher. That is an expectation, not a measurement.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Dataset public (CC BY 4.0, Amazon). Baseline code public.

key_findings.title: SetFit: Efficient Few-Shot Learning Without Prompts (Tunstall, Reimers et al.)
key_findings.what: SetFit fine-tunes a Sentence Transformer contrastively on a few labelled pairs, then trains a classification head on top. Its accuracy is comparable to PEFT/PET few-shot methods, and it trains an order of magnitude faster. The backbones tested range from 15M to 355M parameters. The authors state that it works multilingually when you switch the ST body, for example to a multilingual XLM-R ST.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Best fit for the tier-2 intent classifier: about 45 intents, a few hundred exemplars per intent from templates and translations, minutes of training on one V100. It is also a cheap and honest 'trained on Verda' component.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code public: https://github.com/huggingface/setfit

key_findings.title: intfloat/multilingual-e5-small
key_findings.what: Multilingual embedding model: 12 layers, 384-dim, about 118M parameters, of which about 21.6M are non-embedding. Covers 100 languages (the XLM-R vocabulary), 512-token input. Inputs need the prefix 'query: '. The ONNX int8 version is about 113 MB.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Good backbone for SetFit or kNN intent classification on CPU, at well under 10 ms per question. It covers all EU languages in the dataset, Estonian and Finnish included.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Weights public, MIT licence

key_findings.title: minishlab/potion-multilingual-128M (Model2Vec static embeddings)
key_findings.what: Static embeddings distilled from BAAI/bge-m3 and trained with Tokenlearn on C4 text in 101 languages. 256-dim. The card reports 90.86% of LaBSE's MTEB mean score (47.31 vs 52.07) and calls it 'orders of magnitude faster' on CPU. No absolute throughput figure is given. Released 23 May 2025.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Cheapest possible learned tier: a logistic-regression or kNN head on these embeddings trains in seconds on a laptop and runs in microseconds per question. Use it if the SetFit encoder is too heavy. It is less accurate than a contextual encoder.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Weights public, MIT. Library: https://github.com/MinishLab/model2vec

key_findings.title: XGrammar: Flexible and Efficient Structured Generation Engine for LLMs (Dong et al.)
key_findings.what: Grammar-constrained decoding with byte-level pushdown automata and context-independent token-mask caching. It is up to 100x faster than earlier engines, with near-zero end-to-end overhead and up to 80x end-to-end serving speedup on H100 with Llama-3.1. It is the default structured-output backend in vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM, and it supports JSON, regex and custom CFG.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: If we run a local fine-tuned small LLM (Qwen3-0.6B) as the text-to-DSL fallback, serve it with vLLM plus XGrammar. A JSON schema with an intent enum then makes every output parseable, at no measurable cost.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code public: https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar, Apache-2.0

key_findings.title: Outlines (dottxt-ai)
key_findings.what: Constrained generation library with regex, JSON schema / Pydantic, CFG and choice (Literal/Enum) outputs. Backends: transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, plus OpenAI/Gemini APIs.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: The simplest way to constrain a local Qwen3-0.6B run in plain transformers on a V100, without setting up vLLM. Choice constraints over the intent enum turn the LM into a classifier.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code public, Apache-2.0

key_findings.title: Constrained Decoding Eliminates Structural Failures in Small LLMs but Reveals a Scale-Dependent Semantic Gap (Chavan)
key_findings.what: Five open models from 0.6B to 4B, 14 structured-output tasks, three conditions: native, Outlines, XGrammar. Schema validity rose from 78.6-92.9% native to 100% constrained. Semantic errors, such as multi-step function calling, stay and get worse at smaller scale. The abstract gives no semantic accuracy numbers.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Constrained decoding guarantees valid DSL, not the correct intent. A 0.6B generator still needs fine-tuning on our templates, and its accuracy must be measured on held-out drawings and languages. This is a reason to prefer a classifier plus deterministic slot extraction over free generation.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code: https://github.com/CruiseDevice/small-llm-structured-benchmark (tag v1.0). Licence not stated on the arXiv page.

key_findings.title: SLM-SQL: An Exploration of Small Language Models for Text-to-SQL (Sheng, Xu)
key_findings.what: Qwen2.5-Coder 0.5B-1.5B models, trained with SFT on SynSQL-derived data and then RL, plus corrective self-consistency. BIRD dev execution accuracy: 0.5B 56.87%, 1.5B 67.08%, an average gain of 31.4 points over base. The arXiv page does not report training compute.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Open-domain SQL is far harder than our closed DSL of about 45 intents with verbatim slots, and even there sub-2B models are usable after SFT. A fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B on our template DSL should do much better, but no paper reports numbers for a task like ours.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Authors announce release at https://github.com/CycloneBoy/slm_sql. Licence not stated on the arXiv page.

key_findings.title: Qwen3-0.6B
key_findings.what: Causal LM with 0.6B parameters (0.44B non-embedding), 28 layers, GQA 16/8, 32K context, tied embeddings. Multilingual. Part of the Qwen3 open-weight release.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Candidate for an optional local text-to-DSL fallback that replaces Haiku. A LoRA or full fine-tune on about 15k synthetic pairs fits easily on one V100 16GB or A100. Training time on our data is not reported anywhere and has to be measured.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Weights public, Apache-2.0

key_findings.title: ByT5: Towards a token-free future with pre-trained byte-to-byte models (Xue et al.)
key_findings.what: Byte-level T5 models. The authors report that byte-level models are competitive with token-level ones and significantly more robust to noise and spelling variation.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Only relevant if slot strings come from OCR with noise, for example matching 'PESUH' or 'KPH' read from CubiCasa rasters. For clean typed questions, an encoder classifier with regex slots is cheaper. Treat it as a fallback idea, not the main design.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code and weights released by Google (google-research/byt5). Apache-2.0 per the repo.

key_findings.title: IFC-Bench v2 dataset (Hellin et al.)
key_findings.what: 1,026 free-text QA pairs over 51 IFC models in 22 projects. Categories: direct retrieval 152, computational aggregation 569, geometric/spatial 112, incomplete information 194. Fixed test split of 514. Ground truths are free text from about 25 to 5.9k characters, in mixed units (m, sq m, sq ft, cu m, $). The dataset card reports no baseline accuracy.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: This is where the dataset's ifc_bench family comes from. The answers are free-form, not templated: only 3.2% of the preview's ifc_bench questions matched a held-out template. Route these to the IFC agent, not to the DSL parser. The public train split (512) is usable for few-shot examples.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: QA under CC BY 4.0. IFC models have their own licences: most CC BY/MIT, four GPLv3.

key_findings.title: BIM Information Extraction Through LLM-based Adaptive Exploration (Hellin, Jang, Fuchs, Nousias, Borrmann)
key_findings.what: An LLM agent that runs code on the IFC model and discovers its structure as it goes ('adaptive exploration'). It significantly outperforms static NL-to-query generation in every configuration of a factorial ablation (2 LLM capability levels x 4 augmentation strategies) on ifc-bench v2. The abstract gives no accuracy numbers or model names.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: Supports a hybrid design. Use a fixed DSL for the templated 95%, and do not force the heterogeneous IFC free-text questions into a static query language. The Drawing Desk IFC tool loop is the right home for those.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Benchmark open (see IFC-Bench). Paper CC BY 4.0. Agent code link not on the abstract page.

key_findings.title: Finnish room abbreviations (rakentaja.fi drawing legend)
key_findings.what: Standard list: TK tuulikaappi (vestibule), ET eteinen, K keittiö, KK keittokomero, RT/RH/R ruokailutila, AH asuinhuone, MH makuuhuone, OH olohuone, KH/KPH kylpyhuone, WC, SH suihkuhuone, S sauna, LÖ/L löylyhuone, PE/PH pesuhuone, PU/PKH pukuhuone, KHH kodinhoitohuone, APK apukeittiö, VH vaatehuone, KUI kuivaushuone, ASK askartelutila, VAR varasto, AT/AK autotalli/-katos, TEKN tekninen tila. Conflicts: in the fixture legend, TK also means tankokaappi (wardrobe), L means liesi (stove) and APK means astianpesukone (dishwasher). In housing ads, 'tk' means tupakeittiö (kitchen). Other sources add PARV parveke, TH työhuone, ALK alkovi, MT makuutila, and PESUH as a long form of pesuhuone.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: The CubiCasa intents depend on this lexicon. 'Bathrooms' means KH, KPH, PH, PESUH, SH and excludes WC. 'Kitchens' includes K, KK, avokeittiö, tupakeittiö and APK. 'Bedrooms' means MH. 'Saunas' means S or LÖ. Each DSL intent should carry a label regex for matching against OCR text, and the UI should show that regex. TK is a trap: in a floor-plan room label it means vestibule, not kitchen.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: n/a (reference list)

key_findings.title: CubiCasa5K: A Dataset and an Improved Multi-Task Model for Floorplan Image Analysis (Kalervo et al.)
key_findings.what: 5,000 Finnish floor plans with polygon (SVG) annotations in 80+ categories: 68,877 room instances and 136,676 icon instances. The experiments use 12 room classes (Background, Outdoor, Wall, Kitchen, Living Room, Bedroom, Bath, Hallway, Railing, Storage, Garage, Other) and 11 icon classes. The icon list is reported as Empty, Window, Door, Closet, Electrical Appliance, Toilet, Sink, Sauna Bench, Fire Place, Bathtub, Chimney. I could not check that list fully against the paper. Licence on Zenodo: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: The DSL target classes for raster counting should map one-to-one onto the CubiCasa annotation classes, so the parser's output feeds the detector or segmenter directly. For example, wc_seat maps to Toilet, sink to Sink, sauna to Sauna Bench or the room label S, window to Window, and door to Door. The 'showers and bathtubs' intent needs a check: I did not confirm a separate shower icon class among the 11.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Code and weights: https://github.com/CubiCasa/CubiCasa5k. Data: https://zenodo.org/record/2613548 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

key_findings.title: Swiss Dwellings dataset (Standfest et al., Archilyse)
key_findings.what: Over 45,000 apartments, 370,000 rooms and about 3,100 buildings. geometries.csv holds WKT geometry in metres for areas, walls, railings, columns, windows, doors and features (sinks, bathtubs, ...), with entity_type and entity_subtype (about 80 area subtypes, such as BEDROOM, LIVING_ROOM, KITCHEN, BATHROOM, CORRIDOR, BALCONY, LOGGIA, STAIRCASE, SHAFT). Licence CC BY 4.0.
key_findings.why_it_matters_for_stoa: The question labels are printed room names in DE/FR/IT (Zimmer/Pièce/Stanza, Küche/Cuisine/Cucina, Bad/Bain/Bagno, Korridor/Couloir/Corridoio, Reduit/Réduit/Ripostiglio, Treppenhaus/Cage d'escalier/Vano scala, Balkon/Balcon/Balcone, Loggia, Wohnen/Essen, Séjour/repas, Soggiorno/pranzo, Schlafzimmer/Chambre à coucher/Camera da letto). The source geometry gives the area subtype for each label, which is the ground truth for the 'exclude balconies, loggias, terraces, shafts, voids' filters in the area intents.
key_findings.code_or_weights_available: Data public, CC BY 4.0

concrete_recipe:
Recommendation: a 4-tier cascade. Tier 0 extracts slots with regex. Tier 1 does an exact template lookup. Tier 2 is a multilingual encoder classifier trained on Verda. Tier 3 is Haiku 5.5 with strict structured output. Free-form questions go to the existing Opus/IFC agent. Do not build a seq2seq text-to-DSL model as the main path: in this dataset the slots are verbatim and the intents form a closed set.

DSL (one JSON object per question, about 45 intents):
{intent: enum, op: count|area|sum_area|sum_volume|sum_length|sum_side_area|lookup, target: window|door_with_leaf|door_any|wc_seat|sink|shower_or_bathtub|bathtub|shower|sauna|kitchen|bedroom|bathroom_room|separate_wc_room|storey|apartment|room_by_label|space|wall|slab|column|stair|beam|sanitary_fixture|..., filters: {label?: str (verbatim), room_number?: str, storey?: str, apartment?: str, model?: str, sheet?: str}, exclude: [balcony, loggia, terrace, outdoor, shaft, void]?, unit: count|m2|m3|m|ft2, scope: this_plan|storey|model|schedule, lexicon_regex?: str}.
Each intent maps to one deterministic executor per modality (IFC Qto, DXF polylines and blocks, raster detector, PDF text). For example, bathroom_room has lexicon_regex ^(KH|KPH|PH|PE|PESUH|SH)\b, and WC rooms are excluded.

Steps (about 9-10 h for the core, about 15 h with the stretch goal):
1. Slot extractor (1.5 h, CPU). Write a quote-aware regex for '...', "...", «...» (with or without inner spaces), „...“ and ‘...’, and do not split on in-word apostrophes (d'étage, women's). Also extract room numbers (\d+\.\d+ or (3-1)), 'apartment A/B', sheet ids (A-\d+), units (m², m³, metres, meter, sq ft) and storey names. For IFC labels of the form 'NAME (NUM)', split them so we can match IfcSpace Name/LongName.
2. Intent catalogue (2 h). Hand-label the roughly 45 EN templates: 12 cubicasa, about 14 swiss, about 20 ifc_models. Propagate the labels to the local-language twins automatically: same path, same answer, same slot values. The preview has 1,395 exact EN/local pairs.
3. Tier 1 exact lookup (0.5 h). Normalise the question (lowercase, slots to <Q>/<N>, collapse whitespace) and look it up in a hash table built from all 120k training questions. Measured on the preview with held-out drawings: 95.0% coverage overall (cubicasa 100%, swiss 99.4%, ifc_models 92.0%). Intent accuracy on a hit should be about 100%, because each template maps to one intent by construction. Cost is $0 and about 1 µs per question.
4. Synthetic training data (2 h, Haiku 5.5 Batch API). For each EN template, generate translations into about 30 languages (all EU languages plus the ones present) and about 10 paraphrases each, with slot values sampled from the real label vocabularies (Finnish abbreviations, Swiss DE/FR/IT labels, Estonian/Danish IFC space and storey names). That is about 45 x 30 x 10 = 13.5k pairs. At about 2M output tokens and $0.50/MTok, it costs about $1, or less with batch pricing. Add a held-out language set (for example, translate to 3 languages not in training) to test transfer.
5. Tier 2 classifier (1-2 h, Verda 1V100.4V, $0.24/h, under 1 h of GPU, under $0.50). Use SetFit on intfloat/multilingual-e5-small (MIT, 118M), with masked-slot input 'query: How many rooms labelled <Q> ...'. As a fallback, run logistic regression on potion-multilingual-128M (MIT, CPU, seconds). Evaluate on held-out drawings plus leave-one-language-out. Expected accuracy on templated intents is 98-99% or higher. That is my estimate from the closed template set. It is not measured, so measure it before you claim it. Inference runs on CPU in under 10 ms (ONNX int8, about 113 MB). Set the acceptance threshold on softmax/kNN margin at about 0.85, tuned on the held-out split.
6. Tier 3 Haiku fallback (1 h). Call claude-haiku-5-5 with output_config.format set to a JSON schema with the intent enum, the slot fields, and an 'unsupported' or 'free_form' intent. Keep the intent catalogue as a cached system prefix of about 1.5-2k tokens. Cost at $0.10 input and $0.50 output per MTok: about 2k input plus 80 output tokens, so about $0.00024 per call, or less with cache reads. This tier should see under 5% of questions.
7. Free-form route (no new work). Send ifc_bench and opening_design questions (about 4% of the preview) and questions classified free_form to the existing Opus tool loop and the IFC/DXF native tools. Research (arXiv 2605.01698) supports adaptive exploration over static queries for heterogeneous IFC questions.
8. Verifiability UI (1 h). Render the parse as chips: 'COUNT - bathroom rooms (KH|KPH|PH|PESUH|SH, excluding WC) - this floor plan'. Link each chip to the highlighted span of the question that produced it. Show which tier decided and its confidence. Each executor then shows its evidence: the matched labels, polygons or IFC GUIDs.
9. Optional stretch (4-6 h, Verda 1A100.22V, about 1 h of training, about $2.40). Fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B (Apache-2.0) with LoRA on the 13.5k pairs, text to DSL JSON. Serve it with vLLM plus XGrammar, or Outlines, with the JSON schema enforced, as a $0 local replacement for tier 3. Only do this if tiers 1-2 are finished: published work shows constrained decoding gives 100% valid schema but not correct semantics at 0.6B (arXiv 2609.23742). No published accuracy exists for this kind of DSL, so measure it.

Expected end-to-end parser accuracy: about 99% or higher on templated questions (96% of the preview). Free-form questions are scored by the downstream agent, not by the parser. Blended parser cost: 0.95 x $0 + 0.05 x $0.00024, which is about $0.000012 per question. The parser will not be the accuracy bottleneck: the raster-count executors decide the score, so cap time on this track at about 10 h.
risks: The hidden full set (120k questions, about 30 drawing languages) may contain templates and languages that are not in the preview. Exact lookup then misses, and accuracy depends on the tier-2 translations and the Haiku fallback. Run leave-one-language-out evaluation before you trust the numbers.

Label-match semantics are not defined. Does 'rooms labelled Zimmer' count 'Schlafzimmer' or 'Zimmer 2'? Decide from ground truth (answers in swiss_dwellings), compare exact and token match, and show the rule in the UI.

Quote extraction breaks on in-word apostrophes (d'étage, women's) and on French guillemets with inner spaces (' Pièce '). My quick signature regex already failed on these, so a naive regex silently corrupts slots.

Finnish abbreviation ambiguity. TK is tuulikaappi (vestibule) on drawings, tankokaappi in fixture legends and tupakeittiö (kitchen) in ads. The 'bathroom excluding WC' and 'kitchen including kitchenettes, tupakeittiö, apukeittiö' definitions must match the dataset's ground truth, which was probably derived from CubiCasa SVG room classes, not from printed text.

Unit and scope variants: sq ft in the US opening_design sheets, 'net side area of walls', 'net volume of slabs and plates' (Danish 'dæk og plader'). A wrong op or unit mapping gives a wrong answer even when the intent is correct, because area answers have only 2% tolerance.
Do not overinvest. The parser is a solved part. Executor accuracy (raster counts) dominates the score, so time spent on a seq2seq fine-tune here is time taken from the CV detector.
Most cited accuracy numbers come from other tasks (MASSIVE, ATIS, BIRD). The 98-99% tier-2 figure is an estimate and must be measured on held-out drawings and languages.
CubiCasa5K is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. That is fine for a hackathon, but it limits commercial reuse of any model trained on it (relevant to the Stoa work trial).
Haiku fallback adds latency (hundreds of ms to about 1 s) and an API dependency. Cache the intent catalogue prefix and keep the fallback rate under 5%.
